topics.title: Multiculturalism: recognition, inclusion and common citizenship
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Mandatory syllabus breadth: distinguish the fact of cultural diversity from policies of accommodation, compare recognition with redistribution and balance group protection with individual rights and shared civic participation.

nodes.label: Multiculturalism: recognition and accommodation
Diversity: multiple cultures coexist
Recognition addresses identity-based exclusion
Accommodation and representation tools
Individual rights and shared civic interests
Participation through education, language and work

edges.label: poses a policy question, not an automatic answer
must be tested against individual freedom

tables.title: Distinctions and policy tests

cells: Diversity vs multiculturalism
Diversity describes coexistence; multiculturalism advocates recognition and accommodation.
A diverse city can still have exclusionary institutions.
Recognition vs redistribution
Identity-related disadvantage is not only a resource-allocation problem.
Consider both respectful treatment and material opportunities.
Assimilation vs accommodation
Absorption into majority norms differs from protecting cultural differences.
Enable participation without requiring cultural erasure.
Group rights vs individual rights
Protecting a community can sometimes restrict people within it.
Check internal freedom as well as majority–minority relations.
Symbolic celebration vs substantive inclusion
Public celebration may coexist with unequal education, jobs and voice.
Judge whether recognition changes real opportunities and participation.

tables.title: Cultural diversity and intercultural dialogue (static background, not a new event)

cells: UNESCO's cultural-diversity objective
Use dialogue, recognition and inclusion to structure a multiculturalism answer.
Recognition is not a blanket justification for practices that deny individual rights.
Education and shared knowledge
Explain how education can support communication across groups.
A mandate does not establish a measured reduction in social exclusion.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a city holds a cultural festival but public services remain inaccessible in minority languages. What is the gap?
cards.answer: Symbolic celebration has not resolved substantive access. An illustrative response uses appropriate language access and participation mechanisms while assessing resources and shared civic needs; a festival alone is not inclusion.

cards.question: Why does redistribution alone not exhaust multicultural policy?
cards.answer: Disadvantage can involve disrespect, exclusion from representation and pressure to abandon an identity. Resource transfers may help material conditions without correcting those recognition problems.

cards.question: Illustrative case: a community invokes cultural protection to restrict members' choices. What should an answer test?
cards.answer: Test both protection against majority domination and the individual rights of people within the group. Cultural recognition does not automatically justify internal restrictions; explain the tension rather than rank cultures.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Diversity requires recognition and common citizenship.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: distinguish diversity from a policy stance → explain recognition and material inequality → compare accommodation with assimilation → discuss representation and service access → test group claims against individual rights and common interests → propose substantive participation → evaluate inclusion, not symbolism alone.

cards.question: What is mandatory breadth, and what should not be over-studied?
cards.answer: Prepare diversity/policy, recognition/redistribution and group/individual-right distinctions plus one balanced case. Do not skip it, but avoid memorising every labelled subtype or philosopher; do not reduce communities to fixed stereotypes.

cards.question: Can integration preserve distinct cultures?
cards.answer: Yes, in an accommodation-oriented approach, access to education, language learning, jobs and civic participation need not demand complete absorption into majority cultural practices. The policy test is meaningful participation with rights protection.

cards.question: How can an answer balance cultural recognition and shared citizenship?
cards.answer: Recognise diversity, explain dialogue and access mechanisms, and assess inclusion and individual safeguards. Avoid presenting cultural groups as uniform or inherently in conflict. This is an original learning application of static material, not a reported current event or an official legal interpretation.

topics.title: Urbanisation and migration: drivers, agglomeration and inclusion
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Core depth: distinguish urban population growth from migration alone, explain push–pull drivers and agglomeration, assess origin/destination effects and match urban-service and inclusion policies to real constraints.

nodes.label: Urban change: population, classification and movement
Migration: varied motives and degrees of choice
Push–pull forces: livelihoods, services and safety
Density and connectivity can support productivity
Congestion, housing stress and environmental costs
Infrastructure, land-use planning and inclusion

edges.label: contributes, but is not the only component
requires service capacity to keep pace
can reduce planning and access failures

tables.title: Distinctions and policy tests

cells: Urbanisation vs urban growth
A rising urban share differs from the absolute addition of urban residents.
Check the population base and definition before comparing places.
Natural increase vs migration
Births minus deaths, net movement and reclassification all affect urban totals.
Do not attribute every new urban resident to rural out-migration.
Push vs pull
Origin hardships and destination attractions jointly shape movement.
Diagnose jobs, services, safety and environmental pressures at both ends.
Voluntary vs forced movement
Economic choice differs from displacement with little or no viable option.
Do not treat every migrant as a voluntary job seeker or every displaced person as a cross-border refugee.
Agglomeration vs congestion
Density/connectivity can support productivity; inadequate planning can raise costs.
Judge infrastructure, housing and inclusion rather than assume city growth is automatically developmental.

tables.title: Urban services and disaster resilience (static background, not a new event)

cells: Sendai's risk-reduction focus
Connect exposure and vulnerable services to health, livelihoods and economic losses.
The framework does not demonstrate that migrants cause urban hazards.
Resilient infrastructure
Evaluate how housing and service planning reduce losses for vulnerable residents.
Outcomes require local evidence; an international framework is not an implemented city plan.

tables.title: Scheme design: beneficiaries, delivery and source-era limits

cells: PMAY-U: older scheme description (not PMAY-U 2.0 rules)
Housing and Urban Affairs; pucca housing for eligible urban households including slum dwellers.
Source defines the beneficiary family and a no-pucca-house-anywhere condition; an adult earning member may be separate in this older description.
Older ISSR, CLSS, AHP and BLC routes; ARHCs are mentioned for urban migrants/poor.
The note lists component-specific central assistance and a generic sharing paragraph; their interaction is not resolved here, so no universal funding ratio is taught.

Housing ownership, rental access and loan subsidy tackle different constraints. Do NOT transfer old CLSS/MIG slabs, family rules or subsidy amounts to PMAY-U 2.0. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.
PMAY-U 2.0: version identification only
Housing and Urban Affairs; the visually read ministry mindmap links PMAY-U (2015) to PMAY-U 2.0 (2024).
Eligibility, income bands and exclusions are not supplied by the cited mindmap.
No benefit amounts, verticals or implementation conditions can be established from this version label.
Funding design not established by this page; older PMAY-U funding cannot be silently reused.

Evidence gap is substantive: this source establishes a version label/year, not the current operational guideline. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

cards.question: Illustrative calculation: urban residents increase by 20,000; natural increase is 8,000 and reclassification adds 5,000. What is the residual net migration?
cards.answer: 20,000 - 8,000 - 5,000 = 7,000, assuming these exhaust the components and boundaries are consistently defined. These invented figures show why urban growth is not identical to migration.

cards.question: Illustrative case: workers move after crop failure toward a city with vacancies. Identify push and pull.
cards.answer: Crop failure and fragile livelihoods are origin-side pushes; jobs and income prospects are destination-side pulls. Both can act together, and movement may involve constrained choice rather than a simple preference.

cards.question: Why can migration help an origin region while also creating costs?
cards.answer: Remittances can support household resources, while skilled-worker loss and a changed age composition can create pressures. At destinations, migrants contribute labour but service capacity must adapt; avoid an all-good or all-bad verdict.

cards.question: Plan a descriptive answer: 'Make migration and urbanisation developmental.'
cards.answer: Skeleton: distinguish urban share/growth and movement → decompose urban growth → explain push–pull and agglomeration mechanisms → compare origin/destination benefits and costs → address housing, services, connectivity and participation → discuss planning and displacement trade-offs → assess inclusive productivity and living conditions.

cards.question: What depth is essential, and what should not dominate?
cards.answer: Know the urban-growth decomposition, push–pull, voluntary/forced movement, agglomeration/congestion and origin/destination trade-offs. Prepare a numerical illustration and a policy answer. Do not memorise every city model or use old urban shares; do not blame migrants inherently for service failures.

cards.question: Illustrative case: neighbourhood upgrading raises rents and displaces low-income residents. Why is physical renewal not enough?
cards.answer: The gentrification lens shows that improving buildings and attracting wealth can change living costs and community access. Assess affordability, displacement and inclusive planning alongside investment gains.

cards.question: How would an urban-risk answer include migrants without blaming them for service failures?
cards.answer: Assess housing access, exposure, portability and service capacity. Explain institutional and planning constraints and protect vulnerable residents rather than attributing policy failures to migration itself. This is an original learning application of static material, not a reported current event or an official legal interpretation.

cards.question: Which distinctions would you make in a descriptive answer prompted by a mobility dialogue?
cards.answer: Separate origin/destination, temporary/permanent movement, worker/student channels, rights and coordination. Discuss skills and protection mechanisms without inventing operational immigration permissions. This is an original analytical exercise, not evidence that the initiative achieved its objectives.

cards.question: How would you evaluate an urban transport intervention beyond the number of vehicles or awards?
cards.answer: Assess access time and cost, reliability, integration, safety and inclusion for vulnerable residents. Explain which constraints the intervention addresses and use outcome evidence rather than ceremonial recognition. This is an original analytical exercise, not evidence that the initiative achieved its objectives.

cards.question: Original illustrative mini-case: a borrower applies an older PMAY-U CLSS subsidy slab to PMAY-U 2.0 because the names are similar. Is the inference supported?
cards.answer: No. Part 2 describes older ISSR/CLSS/AHP/BLC; the visually read mindmap separately labels PMAY-U 2.0 as 2024. That label does not establish 2.0 income bands, benefits, verticals or eligibility. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

cards.question: Why might housing ownership assistance alone miss an urban migrant's immediate housing constraint?
cards.answer: A mobile worker may need affordable rental access rather than a purchase loan or an owned house. The source explicitly mentions ARHCs for urban migrants and poor; this does not establish any individual's current rental eligibility. Source-era only; verify current guideline. Operational status uncertain; undated notes are not current certification.

updates.title: Migration: distinguish international mobility from urbanisation
updates.body: The compilation reports an India-Canada Migration and Mobility Dialogue involving students, skilled workers, professionals and business visitors. This is a useful reminder that migration is not only rural-to-urban movement. A dialogue or terms of reference is not automatically a new visa entitlement or evidence of higher migration flows. October 2026 is the compilation edition, not an independently verified release or effective date. Verify the original release before using event details as facts.

updates.title: Urban mobility: accessibility, inclusion and integration
updates.body: The compilation describes an Urban Mobility India conference focused on accessibility and liveability. Use the item to connect transport integration, affordability and access to jobs/services. A conference theme, award or technology demonstration does not prove a city has resolved congestion or exclusion. October 2026 is the compilation edition, not an independently verified release or effective date. Verify the original release before using event details as facts.

topics.title: National income: boundaries, bridges and welfare
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Identify the production boundary, reconcile measurement approaches and distinguish output growth from welfare.

nodes.label: National accounts: production, income and expenditure
Boundary: resident, territory and current production
Three methods: value added, factor income, final expenditure
Domestic → national; gross → net; valuation basis
Nominal versus real output and GDP deflator
Per-capita output is not distribution or environmental welfare
Base-year and data revisions change comparability

edges.label: prevents double counting and transfer-income errors
reconciles aggregates on the same basis
separates price change from output change
real growth still leaves welfare gaps
requires consistent series and base-year labels

tables.title: Distinctions and application checks

cells: Domestic / national
Territory of production / income of residents.
Residence is an economic concept, not citizenship; use NFIA only for the national bridge.
Gross / net
Subtract consumption of fixed capital (depreciation) to obtain the net aggregate.
Do not subtract depreciation twice.
Factor cost / basic prices / market prices
The notes distinguish factor payments, production taxes/subsidies and product taxes/subsidies.
Do not equate GVA at basic prices with GDP at market prices without the appropriate tax/subsidy bridge.
Value added / income / expenditure
Subtract intermediate inputs / sum factor incomes / count final uses.
All three need compatible boundaries and valuations; share trades themselves are not fresh production.
Nominal / real / deflator
Current-price value / constant-price output / nominal-to-real price index.
Deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100; an index level of 125 is not 125% inflation.
National income / disposable income
Earned factor income differs from resources available after relevant transfers and taxes.
A remittance can affect disposable resources without being current domestic production.

cards.question: A used machine is resold through a broker. What belongs in current production?
cards.answer: The old machine's resale value is not newly produced output; the current brokerage service is. Classify the transaction before adding money flows.

cards.question: Original illustrative calculation: a grower sells produce for 80, a processor sells for 150 and a retailer sells for 190. Assume no other intermediate inputs. Find total value added.
cards.answer: Value added = 80 + (150 − 80) + (190 − 150) = 190 currency units, not gross sales of 420. Invented inputs demonstrate the anti-double-counting rule; they are not source statistics.

cards.question: Original illustrative bridge: GDP at market prices 1,000; depreciation 80; net indirect taxes 100; NFIA −20. Find textbook NNP at factor cost.
cards.answer: 1,000 − 80 − 100 − 20 = 800. State every valuation and sign. These invented figures use the notes' textbook factor-cost bridge, not a claim that today's headline GDP is reported at factor cost.

cards.question: Original illustrative price calculation: nominal GDP 600 and real GDP 480. What is the deflator?
cards.answer: 600 ÷ 480 × 100 = 125 index points. It means the aggregate price level is 25% above the reference level of 100; computing annual inflation would also require the preceding period's index.

cards.question: Can an Indian passport alone establish inclusion in India's national income?
cards.answer: No. Distinguish citizenship from economic residence and distinguish factor income from transfers. The notes' shorthand about 'Indians/foreigners' must be read with their residence definition.

cards.question: Plan an answer: 'GDP growth is necessary but insufficient for development.'
cards.answer: Outline: define real output → explain measurement and production boundaries → distinguish per-capita output from distribution → discuss unpaid services and environmental costs → conclude with complementary welfare indicators and careful comparisons. Use an official dated release for any contemporary number.

cards.question: How deep should this P1 topic be studied, and where should revision stop?
cards.answer: Master three methods, final/intermediate classification, gross/net and domestic/national bridges, basic-price versus market-price labels, disposable-income distinctions, real/nominal/deflator and welfare limits. Stop after solving fresh mixed cases without cues; do not memorise historical per-capita figures or obsolete sector weights. P1 is a study allocation, not permission to omit any syllabus chapter.

cards.question: Which statements in these notes require a source check before use?
cards.answer: The early blanket GVA = GDP wording conflicts with the later distinction between basic-price GVA and market-price GDP. Later pages also mix a newer base-year assertion with the earlier series discussion. Treat release status/base year as date-sensitive and check NSO; do not repeat citizenship shorthand, declare all non-market production excluded, or infer that nominal GDP has no policy use.

cards.question: How can environmental accounts improve an ESI answer without claiming GDP measures all welfare?
cards.answer: Explain what conventional output measures omit, identify the relevant resource stock/flow, and discuss comparable data and valuation limits. Better measurement can inform policy; it does not itself solve resource degradation. This is an original analytical exercise, not evidence that the initiative achieved its objectives.

updates.title: Environmental-economic accounting: connect output to resource use
updates.body: The supplied compilation reports a MoSPI environmental-economic accounting strategy for 2026-30, covering resource and environmental accounts and data gaps. Link this to GDP's measurement boundaries and the difference between production, natural assets and welfare. Do not equate an accounting strategy with a completed green-GDP estimate or an achieved environmental outcome. October 2026 is the compilation edition, not an independently verified release or effective date. Verify the original release before using event details as facts.

topics.title: Economic reforms: stabilisation, incentives and inclusion
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Explain the crisis-to-reform mechanism and assess efficiency gains alongside distributional and employment concerns.

nodes.label: Reforms: stabilise the economy and change incentives
Crisis: fiscal stress, external vulnerability and shocks
Stabilisation: inflation, fiscal and external balance
Liberalisation, privatisation and global integration
Structural reform: competition, finance and productive capacity
Assessment: growth, jobs, agriculture, inequality and human development

edges.label: opens entry, ownership and international channels
must be evaluated beyond aggregate growth

tables.title: Distinctions and application checks

cells: Stabilisation / structural adjustment
Contain near-term imbalances / alter long-run supply incentives and institutions.
Tax and financial changes can serve both; the categories are analytical, not watertight.
Liberalisation / absence of regulation
Reduce restrictive entry and controls, not every public-interest rule.
Ask what competition and supervision replace administrative controls.
Disinvestment / privatisation
Selling equity need not transfer control; privatisation involves private ownership/control.
Check the actual transaction rather than treating every share sale as privatisation.
PSU autonomy / ownership transfer
More managerial discretion can occur without selling an enterprise.
Understand the incentive rationale; do not memorise changing Ratna thresholds.
Current-account / capital-account convertibility
Routine international transactions differ from investment and borrowing flows.
Do not infer unrestricted capital mobility from trade liberalisation; source descriptions contain simplified categories.
Efficiency / inclusion
Growth, investment and exports are not the same test as jobs, regional balance and social access.
Use balanced mechanisms and dated evidence, not a claim that every outcome was caused solely by reforms.

tables.title: Reform mechanism: recommendations, implementation and outcomes (static background, not a new event)

cells: Competition and control
Banking-reform discussions illustrate how market structure and regulatory design can change incentives.
A proposed change is not evidence that it was implemented.
Consolidation
Institutional scale and ownership are separate from performance outcomes.
Evaluate efficiency, access and safeguards instead of assuming larger banks are always better.

tables.title: IBC: reallocation and creditor coordination (retrospective; date unspecified)

cells: Insolvency resolution
A framework can support asset-value preservation, creditor coordination and the exit/restructuring of distressed businesses.
The supplied summary is not a substitute for current legislation or case-specific legal rules.
Amendment discussion
The source describes a 2026 bill and proposed changes.
Bill passage, enactment and commencement are distinct. Its status and precise thresholds are not independently verified; no effective date is invented.

cards.question: How could an oil-price shock aggravate an already vulnerable external position?
cards.answer: A higher import bill and weaker remittance inflows can intensify foreign-exchange pressure. Explain interaction with domestic fiscal and industrial weaknesses, rather than reciting a crisis-year statistics list.

cards.question: The government sells a small shareholding but retains control. Is this necessarily privatisation?
cards.answer: No. It is disinvestment; whether control actually transfers is the relevant distinction. Greater PSU autonomy is another reform lever and is not itself a sale.

cards.question: Why might competition gains coexist with pressure on some workers or sectors?
cards.answer: Opening markets can improve efficiency and export opportunities while import competition, skill mismatch and uneven access to services leave adjustment costs concentrated. Identify affected groups and complementary policy rather than making an all-good/all-bad judgement.

cards.question: Outline: 'The next stage of reform must convert growth into broad development.'
cards.answer: Crisis and objectives briefly → stabilisation versus structural changes → LPG transmission through incentives and finance → gains and adjustment costs → employment, agriculture, infrastructure, skills, governance and sustainability → balanced conclusion.

cards.question: What does P2 breadth require here?
cards.answer: Cover crisis mechanisms, LPG distinctions, stabilisation/structural horizons, ownership versus control, convertibility and a balanced evaluation. Stop before detailed chronology, successive licensing lists or Ratna numeric criteria. Practise a policy-comparison answer; the whole syllabus remains mandatory breadth, and P2 is not a prediction of question frequency.

cards.question: Which reform claims should not be carried forward unqualified?
cards.answer: The notes use sweeping claims about removal of trade barriers and broad causal claims about sectoral outcomes. Do not treat them as current legal rules or causal proof. Use the fiscal-policy packet rather than page 11's loose deficit definition; verify present trade/investment restrictions and any modern scheme before naming its scope.

cards.question: Structure a critical answer using a historical committee recommendation.
cards.answer: Name the problem and proposed mechanism; distinguish enacted measures from proposals; evaluate outcomes and limitations with appropriate evidence; conclude without treating the recommendation as a current rule. This is an original learning application of static material, not a reported current event or an official legal interpretation.

cards.question: Illustrative ESI prompt: why can an insolvency framework matter beyond bank recovery?
cards.answer: Explain coordination, the preservation/reallocation of productive assets and orderly exit. Then discuss delay and implementation capacity. Do not assume the source's amendment proposals are in force; exact legal rules need verification.

topics.title: Nature of the Indian economy: transformation and persistent gaps
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Assess development using structural change, capabilities and distribution, not a single income ranking.

nodes.label: Developing economy: progress alongside structural constraints
Income: aggregate and per-person measures
Structure: sectoral output and employment need separate checks
Distribution: inequality, poverty and the Lorenz/Gini lens
Capabilities: health, education, skills and productive work
Capacity: capital, infrastructure, technology and finance

edges.label: average gains do not establish equal gains
skills and job opportunities affect labour movement

tables.title: Distinctions and application checks

cells: Growth / development
Higher output is quantitative; development also involves structural and social improvement.
Use income and structural indicators together.
Output share / employment share
A sector can lose GDP share faster than it releases labour.
Do not equate services-led output growth with complete labour transformation.
Per-capita income / inequality
An average says little about how income or wealth is shared.
Specify whether an inequality estimate concerns income, consumption or wealth.
Lorenz curve / Gini
Cumulative distribution picture / area-based inequality summary.
Gini = area between equality line and Lorenz curve ÷ area under equality line; compare consistent concepts.
Human / physical capital
Health, schooling and skills / equipment and infrastructure.
Both matter for productivity; neither is captured adequately by a headline rank alone.
Structural / cyclical unemployment
Mismatch and slow reallocation / fluctuations in aggregate activity.
Recognise mechanisms without asserting that one form is absent in India.

cards.question: If services' GDP share rises while many workers remain in agriculture, what should an answer investigate?
cards.answer: The gap between output and employment transformation, productivity, skills and non-farm opportunities. A falling agricultural output share alone does not demonstrate adequate job creation elsewhere.

cards.question: Original illustrative geometry: area under equality line = 0.50; area between it and the Lorenz curve = 0.15. Find Gini.
cards.answer: Gini = 0.15 ÷ 0.50 = 0.30. These invented areas show the formula only; they are not an estimate for India. Gini alone cannot reveal the poverty level or mean income.

cards.question: Explain the low-capital/low-income feedback without treating it as destiny.
cards.answer: Low capital can constrain productivity and income; low income can limit saving and investment. Better human capital, infrastructure and financial intermediation provide channels for change. Evaluate the constraints rather than claiming that every household is trapped identically.

cards.question: Outline: 'India combines signs of underdevelopment with sustained structural progress.'
cards.answer: Define the evaluation criteria → income and distribution → output/employment mismatch → human capital and technology constraints → infrastructure and finance progress → conclude with a multidimensional, evidence-qualified assessment.

cards.question: Where should P2 study stop?
cards.answer: Be able to defend the developing-economy assessment using income, sectoral/employment, inequality, capabilities and capital/finance lenses. Learn Lorenz/Gini interpretation, not a country-rank list. Stop after one balanced outline and a fresh structural-change case. Whole-syllabus breadth is still compulsory; priority is not an exam-frequency claim.

cards.question: How should report rankings, poverty figures and demographic labels be revised?
cards.answer: Record publisher, income/wealth/poverty concept, reference period and population before comparing. The notes mix multiple poverty measures and report vintages; do not combine them into one trend. Their dated national targets and simplified human-capital/unemployment statements need checking, not rote reuse.

topics.title: Post-1991 macroeconomy: growth, capital formation and delivery
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Connect services-led growth and household saving to investment, while examining employment, regional and project-delivery gaps.

nodes.label: Post-reform macroeconomy: growth quality as well as pace
Services-led output transformation
Per-capita income: an average, not a distribution
Saving → mobilisation of finance → investment
Capital formation: fixed assets and inventories
Public/private delivery: PPP, viability support and social investment

edges.label: does not settle who shares the gains
must weigh efficiency, access and long-contract risk

tables.title: Distinctions and application checks

cells: GDP growth / per-capita income
Aggregate output expansion / average per person.
Neither establishes equal gains across people or regions.
Sectoral output / labour absorption
Fast service growth can coexist with pressure on agricultural livelihoods.
Discuss output/employment mismatch rather than assuming automatic job transfer.
Saving / finance / investment
Resources not consumed / intermediation / addition to productive assets.
A higher saving pool still needs mobilisation and viable investment opportunities.
Fixed capital / change in inventories
Longer-lived productive assets / changes in stocks of materials and goods.
Do not call every capital-formation component a new factory.
PPP / viability gap support
A public-private project arrangement / fiscal support for viability.
Risk-sharing and access must be checked; public support does not eliminate project risk.
Commercial project partnership / CSR
Infrastructure delivery contract / corporate social-responsibility investment.
Do not confuse contractual returns with a social-spending obligation; applicability is date-sensitive.

cards.question: Why can a rise in household saving fail to produce an equal immediate rise in productive investment?
cards.answer: The notes distinguish saving, financial mobilisation and actual investment. Discuss the intermediation and project-delivery steps rather than assuming that a saving statistic proves productive assets were created.

cards.question: Original illustrative calculation: real income rises from 1,000 to 1,100 units while population rises from 100 to 105. What happens to per-capita income?
cards.answer: It rises from 10 to about 10.48 units: (1,100 ÷ 105) ÷ (1,000 ÷ 100) − 1 ≈ 4.76%. Aggregate growth of 10% is not per-capita growth. Inputs are invented and say nothing about distribution.

cards.question: A PPP bid promises low fiscal cost but high user charges and uncertain long-term demand. What are the checks?
cards.answer: Assess efficiency and expertise gains alongside affordability, aggressive bidding, duration and risk allocation. Viability support is a financing tool, not evidence that every PPP is socially accessible or commercially sound.

cards.question: Outline: 'Assess the quality of India's post-reform growth.'
cards.answer: Brief growth direction without a year-by-year list → services and employment mismatch → per-capita and regional distribution → saving-finance-investment chain → public/private delivery and access → balanced conclusion and dated official evidence.

cards.question: How much post-1991 chronology is enough for P2?
cards.answer: Know services-led transformation, income/distribution limits, saving/investment components and PPP/VGF/CSR distinctions. Stop before plan-period growth tables and acronym catalogues; practise one project-risk case. Retain the whole syllabus's mandatory breadth rather than using P2 to skip this area.

cards.question: Which claims should not be treated as settled current facts?
cards.answer: The GDP-overestimation discussion presents a disputed argument and blurs price basis with real measurement; do not repeat it as established fact. The page 9 blanket criticism of social-sector PPP feasibility sits beside a description of social-sector viability support: use case-specific assessment. Refresh investment data and CSR/scheme applicability from current official material.

topics.title: Public expenditure and receipts: classify before evaluating
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Separate accounting classification, economic purpose and financing consequences when assessing public finances.

nodes.label: Public finances: what is spent and how it is financed
Expenditure: revenue and capital classification
Purpose: development and service delivery
Transfers versus purchase of current goods/services
Receipts: tax, non-tax and capital flows
Quality: composition, scale and spending management

edges.label: is distinct from judging development value
also distinguishes redistribution from direct purchases
classifies funding without calling borrowing income
evaluates spending relative to resources and outcomes

tables.title: Distinctions and application checks

cells: Revenue / capital expenditure
Operating and other non-asset expenditure / asset creation or liability reduction.
Recurring versus one-off is only a clue, not the decisive test; spending quality is a separate question.
Grant for assets / direct capital spending
A grant and the recipient's eventual asset creation are not the same accounting entry.
The expenditure notes list asset grants under capital, but the fiscal notes explicitly classify central grants as revenue even when intended for assets; use the latter distinction.
Developmental / non-developmental labels
An older purpose-based grouping differs from revenue/capital accounting.
Do not infer that education salaries lack development value or every administrative service is socially useless.
Transfer / non-transfer expenditure
Redistribution without a current service in return / payment for current goods and services.
A welfare payment is not itself production; the recipient's later purchase is a different transaction.
Tax / non-tax revenue receipts
Compulsory taxes / receipts such as interest and dividends.
Neither borrowing nor disinvestment belongs in ordinary revenue receipts.
Debt / non-debt capital receipts
Borrowing creates a repayment liability; loan recovery and disinvestment reduce assets.
A non-debt receipt is not automatically recurrent or proof of improved fiscal capacity.

tables.title: Report evidence: framework, India application and verification

cells: Ministry of Finance / Union Budget 2026-27 (claimed)
The compilation distinguishes estimated receipts/expenditure, revenue/capital categories and Budget versus Revised Estimates.
Classify each fiscal item before evaluating development priorities; compare BE with BE or explicitly identify the change in estimate status.

Capital spending is not automatically effective and revenue spending is not automatically waste. The introductory classification is broad; legal authorisation and accounting treatment require primary documents.

cards.question: Classify new machinery, its maintenance and interest on the borrowing used to buy it.
cards.answer: Direct acquisition creates a capital asset; routine maintenance and interest are revenue expenditure. An expense's usefulness does not change its accounting class. The fiscal notes supply the sharper asset/liability test.

cards.question: The government receives a dividend, recovers an old loan and issues a new bond. Are these all revenue receipts?
cards.answer: No: dividend is non-tax revenue; loan recovery is non-debt capital receipt; bond borrowing is debt-creating capital receipt. Separate operating resources, asset reduction and future liabilities.

cards.question: Original illustrative calculation: spending rises from 200 to 230 units while nominal GDP rises from 1,000 to 1,250. Has spending/GDP increased?
cards.answer: It falls from 20% to 18.4%, despite spending increasing 15%. Invented figures demonstrate why absolute spending alone is insufficient; examine composition and real service delivery as well.

cards.question: Outline: 'The quality of expenditure matters as much as its size.'
cards.answer: Define the revenue/capital and transfer classifications → separate them from development purpose → compare spending/GDP and composition → discuss infrastructure, health, education and implementation → connect financing to fiscal/debt constraints → conclude with an outcome-based assessment.

cards.question: What should P1 expenditure revision cover?
cards.answer: Practise mixed expenditure/receipt classifications, transfer-versus-purchase cases and asset/liability consequences; distinguish productive social spending from accounting capital expenditure. Stop before historical spending totals or lengthy Planning Commission chronology. P1 depth complements, not substitutes for, mandatory whole-syllabus breadth.

cards.question: What are the important source limitations?

Their capital-grant listing conflicts with the fiscal notes. Institutional descriptions of NITI Aayog also need verification before implying it allocates funds like the former Planning Commission.

cards.question: Recall: why must a fiscal comparison retain BE, RE and actual-status labels?
cards.answer: BE is a budget plan; RE revises that plan as information improves; neither is a final outturn. A change in the estimate label can otherwise be mistaken for a realised spending change.

cards.question: Original illustrative calculation: debt 600, GDP 1,000, annual interest 36 and revenue receipts 180. Compute two burden indicators.
cards.answer: Debt/GDP = 60%; interest/revenue receipts = 20%. If debt becomes 630 and GDP 1,100, debt/GDP falls to about 57.27% even though the stock rises. Inputs are invented; none establishes a universal safe-debt threshold.

cards.question: Why can replacing a maturing bond solve a cash problem without solving a debt problem?
cards.answer: New borrowing can repay old principal, shifting the maturity profile without reducing total obligations. Check the new interest terms and future rollover concentration.

cards.question: Does borrowing for a useful project make servicing risk disappear?
cards.answer: No. Productive use can strengthen capacity and future resources, while interest and repayment obligations still require financing. Compare benefits, debt-service pressure and alternative uses of funds; avoid the notes' overly categorical 'not a burden' wording.

cards.question: Outline: 'Debt sustainability is more than the debt/GDP ratio.'
cards.answer: Define government coverage and valuation → debt/GDP and interest/revenue burden → maturity and currency exposure → purpose and growth contribution → refinancing/debt-management options → fiscal capacity and risks → conditional conclusion.

cards.question: Why retain P2 while still learning debt mechanisms?
cards.answer: This packet retains P2 breadth: understand indicators, maturity/currency risks, financing use, three government funds and management tools. Its links to P1 fiscal policy justify applied cases, not a separate promotion or an exam-frequency claim. Stop before old targets, redemption catalogues and institutional date lists; all syllabus chapters still require breadth.

cards.question: Which source statements need caution?
cards.answer: The source mixes wider national external-debt instruments with government debt and treats improving ratios as near-conclusive evidence of sustainability. It also simplifies monetary financing and debt definitions. Define coverage, currency valuation and observation date; do not import historical targets, current ratios or treat currency issuance as a costless routine debt solution.

cards.question: Application: can two states with equal debt/GSDP face different repayment pressure?
cards.answer: Yes. Compare interest burdens relative to receipts, own-revenue capacity, committed expenditure and reliance on transfers. An identical stock ratio does not imply identical fiscal space.

Market borrowing / monetary financing
Raise funds through debt markets / financing involving central-bank money.

Stabilisation / consolidation

Consider timing, composition, vulnerable groups and the monetary stance instead of indiscriminate cuts.

cards.question: Original illustrative budget (same units): total expenditure 500, revenue expenditure 350, revenue receipts 300, non-debt capital receipts 20, interest 40 and asset-creation grants 15. Find four deficits.
cards.answer: Fiscal = 500 − 300 − 20 = 180; revenue = 350 − 300 = 50; primary = 180 − 40 = 140 (interest as defined in this practice budget); effective revenue = 50 − 15 = 35. All inputs are invented; borrowing is not subtracted as a receipt in the fiscal-deficit formula.

cards.question: Is deficit spending always inflationary or always harmful to private investment?
cards.answer: No automatic verdict follows. The notes identify idle-capacity utilisation and infrastructure benefits as well as inflation, servicing and crowding-out risks. Explain the financing channel, resource constraints and spending composition rather than turning a possible effect into an identity.

cards.question: How can fiscal and monetary choices pull in opposite directions during inflation?
cards.answer: Fiscal demand support can add to spending pressure while monetary tightening seeks to restrain credit and demand. Distinguish targeted relief or supply-improving expenditure from broad stimulus, and explain the growth/inflation trade-off. This is an analytical application of the notes, not a claim about a current Budget or RBI decision.

cards.question: Why have fiscal rules and an escape provision together?
cards.answer: Rules support discipline and transparent medium-term expectations; exceptional shocks may justify a disclosed deviation rather than pretending circumstances never change. Explain safeguards and the return to a sustainable path, without treating an old numeric target as current law.

cards.question: Outline: 'Fiscal consolidation should improve quality, not merely shrink expenditure.'
cards.answer: Define deficit and debt sustainability → allocation/distribution/stabilisation functions → revenue mobilisation and expenditure composition → financing/crowding-out risks → fiscal-monetary coordination → transparent rules and shock flexibility → balanced way forward.

cards.question: What is the P1 stopping rule for fiscal policy?
cards.answer: Solve a mixed-budget deficit problem, justify classification choices, compare financing channels and discuss consolidation with a growth/equity trade-off. Know FRBM's rationale and disclosure/escape logic, not every amendment-year target. Stop after a clean case and descriptive outline; continue mandatory breadth elsewhere in the syllabus.

cards.question: Which fiscal details must be refreshed before a current-affairs answer?

The source alternates 'net interest liabilities' and broader interest language and contains simplified monetary-financing statements. Verify official definitions and current legal exceptions; no current target or rate is asserted by this packet.

cards.question: Answer framework: design a fiscally credible response to an energy-price shock.
cards.answer: Original outline: identify transmission to inflation and real incomes; target temporary household relief; assess fiscal space and incentives; set an exit trigger; coordinate monetary and financial-stability policy. Do not present the PDF recommendation as implemented Indian policy.

cards.question: A tax is collected by the Union. Must the Union retain its entire proceeds?
cards.answer: No. Levy, collection and appropriation can be assigned differently. Identify the constitutional sharing route, its exclusions and the relevant recommendation before describing who receives what.

cards.question: A question asks how to supplement municipal resources. Which Finance Commission function is relevant?
cards.answer: Measures to augment the state's Consolidated Fund to supplement resources of municipalities, alongside the equivalent panchayat function. Explain this route rather than confusing it with direct GST administration.

cards.question: Why is a conditional grant not identical to general tax devolution?
cards.answer: The source distinguishes assigned/shared taxes from grant channels; a grant's purpose and conditions need separate examination. For a contemporary scheme, establish who is eligible, which tier finances it and what conditions/exclusions apply instead of assuming every state receives an identical unconditional transfer.

cards.question: Outline: 'Fiscal federalism requires both autonomy and coordination.'
cards.answer: Division of responsibilities and tax powers → levy/collection/retention distinction → Union-state sharing and inter-state distribution → grants and local-body support → GST coordination and borrowing constraints → transparent cooperative arrangements.

cards.question: Why P2, and what must still be mastered?
cards.answer: Retain P2 breadth: understand assignment/sharing/grants, Finance Commission functions, GST Council contrast and borrowing qualification. Fiscal-policy links warrant application practice, not a priority promotion. Stop before exhaustive article/committee chronology or changing devolution weights. cards.question: What source-specific legal caveats matter?
cards.answer: Do not reproduce the blanket claim that every state loan needs Union consent as the complete law. Also verify the source's wording on Article 275 beneficiary groups, emergency transfer powers and examples of abolished taxes before a legal answer. The latest Finance Commission report must be read separately; this static packet asserts no current sharing percentage.

cards.question: Why does a Centre-state policy answer need both responsibility and resources?
cards.answer: Identify the function and delivery actors, then examine financing, capacity and coordination. Keep legislative competence distinct from taxes, grants and actual expenditure. This is an original learning application of static material, not a reported current event or an official legal interpretation.

cards.question: Recall: distinguish vertical and horizontal devolution.
cards.answer: Vertical devolution sets the collective state share relative to the Union; horizontal devolution allocates that state share among individual states. Keep the two stages separate; this PDF's numerical recommendations remain unverified.

cards.answer: Banks help channel funds from surplus holders to deficit-spending sectors, supporting expenditure, investment and employment. Credit appraisal and repayment capacity remain relevant: channelising funds is not proof every project is productive.

cards.question: Original illustrative reserve arithmetic: a toy bank receives 2,500 units and retains an assumed 8%. How much remains in this first-round example?

cards.question: Recall: is the supplied FSR framework an assessment of financial stability or proof of inclusive credit access?

Understand KCC and support schemes by scope, not stale limits. Stop before detailed institutional chronology or rigid group-size lists. Keep mandatory breadth across the rest of the syllabus.

topics.title: Inflation: measurement, causes and limits of policy
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Identify the relevant price measure and shock before explaining monetary transmission and the growth-price trade-off.

nodes.label: Inflation: a change in the general price level
Measurement: consumer, wholesale and producer-price lenses
Demand-pull: expenditure outpaces supply
Cost-push and imported shocks: input prices and exchange rates
Policy transmission: rates/liquidity → finance → spending
Limits: supply constraints and stagflation create trade-offs

edges.label: requires a defined basket, base and period
can restrain credit and spending pressure
can combine higher prices with weaker activity
requires qualified rather than automatic policy claims

tables.title: Distinctions and application checks

cells: Deflation / disinflation
A falling general price level / a slower rate of price increase.
Slower positive inflation still means prices are rising; it need not end at zero.
Headline / core
A broad consumer basket / a measure excluding specified volatile components.
Exclusion is a basket/weight choice, not simple subtraction of headline and food inflation percentages.
CPI / WPI
Consumer-basket prices including services / wholesale commodity prices without services in the notes.
Scope, weights and production/retail stage differ, so the two rates need not match.
Demand-pull / cost-push
Expenditure pressure / higher costs or supply disruption.
Diagnose the shock; monetary restraint cannot directly manufacture missing supply.
Global import-price rise / currency depreciation
Foreign-currency price increase / greater domestic-currency cost for a given foreign price.
Either can raise local costs; pass-through and trade effects should not be assumed identical in every episode.
Rate/liquidity tools / supply-side response
Influence financing and demand / address the cost or availability problem.
Stagflation makes the output-price trade-off explicit; fiscal and monetary choices must be considered together.

tables.title: Report evidence: framework, India application and verification

cells: Joint UN agencies / SOFI 2026 (claimed)
Cost of a Healthy Diet estimates the least cost of a nutritionally adequate basket, subject to price coverage and update limits.
For India, use it as a nutrition-affordability lens alongside, not in place of, CPI; local and seasonal price differences matter for household vulnerability.
A diet-cost level is not a CPI inflation rate. Do not compare PPP-denominated cost levels across years without checking price bases and methodology; global values are omitted.
IMF / WEO July 2026 update (claimed)
The policy discussion links persistent inflation, expectations and exchange-rate pass-through to a tighter stance, while easing is conditional on weaker growth and subsiding price pressure.
Illustrative India application: distinguish a first-round supply shock from second-round inflation and choose policy conditional on persistence and credibility.
Not an RBI policy decision or an automatic rate rule. General recommendations and the purported July 2026 context remain unverified.

cards.question: Original illustrative CPI calculation: a fixed basket costs 800 in the base period, 960 last year and 1,008 now. Compute index and annual inflation.
cards.answer: Current CPI = 1,008 ÷ 800 × 100 = 126; previous CPI = 120. Annual inflation = (126 − 120) ÷ 120 × 100 = 5%, not 26%. The costs and period labels are invented; 26% is the rise from the base, not the last year's inflation.

cards.question: Inflation falls from 8% to 5%. Have prices necessarily fallen?
cards.answer: No. This is disinflation if the inflation rate remains positive: the general price level is still increasing, just more slowly. Deflation refers to a negative rate of general price change.

cards.question: An imported input becomes costly while growth weakens. Why is simply raising rates an incomplete answer?
cards.answer: Rate increases work through finance and demand; they do not directly reverse the input shortage. The notes' imported-inflation and stagflation discussion motivates weighing inflation control against weaker output, with targeted fiscal/supply responses analysed separately. This is an original policy case, not a current policy recommendation.

cards.question: Trace a monetary-tightening mechanism and give its stopping point.
cards.answer: Higher policy funding costs or liquidity withdrawal can make credit conditions tighter and moderate spending pressure. Do not promise a one-for-one lending-rate or price response: the mechanism acts through financial decisions, while imported costs and supply constraints may remain. The notes explain instruments, not a quantified transmission model.

cards.question: Outline: 'Managing inflation requires correct diagnosis and a coherent policy mix.'
cards.answer: Define inflation and the index/period → distinguish demand, supply and imported shocks → explain rate/liquidity transmission → discuss purchasing power and stagflation → fiscal/supply-side complements and policy trade-offs → conclude with dated, scope-matched evidence.

cards.question: What should P1 inflation depth cover?
cards.answer: Solve index-versus-rate and disinflation cases, compare CPI/WPI/core, identify the shock, trace transmission and explain its limits and fiscal interaction. Stop before obsolete weights, base years, daily rates and country 'ideal misery-index' ranges. Whole-syllabus breadth remains mandatory even when this topic receives deeper practice.

cards.question: What must be checked rather than learned verbatim?
cards.answer: The PDF contains an older inflation-target period, stale base-year/weight claims, an undated stagflation assessment and simplified operational descriptions. Do not use its SLR asset list or repo wording as a precise current legal definition, or assume its reverse-repo description is today's full liquidity corridor. Verify current RBI/NSO releases; this packet asserts no present target, base year or rate.

cards.question: Application: can healthy-diet affordability worsen even if headline inflation slows?
cards.answer: Yes. Slower inflation need not lower the price level or raise household purchasing power. Diet composition, local prices, availability and income matter; use the PDF framework rather than an invented India statistic.

topics.title: Indian taxation: design, GST mechanics and revenue responsiveness
topics.subject: ESI
topics.summary: Compare tax design and compliance mechanisms, apply input-credit logic and interpret revenue responsiveness without relying on stale slabs.

nodes.label: Taxation: revenue with equity and efficient administration
Design: fairness, adequacy, simplicity and transparency
Types: direct/indirect and progressive/proportional/regressive
GST: value addition, input credit and destination
Compliance: source deduction, information and anti-abuse tools
Responsiveness: revenue growth relative to GDP
Institutions: GST Council, tax authorities and GSTN

edges.label: balances revenue and distribution with compliance costs
changes who is legally liable and how burdens vary
uses input-credit links to reduce cascading
supports collection and limits concealment or abuse
tests how revenue moves with the economy
coordinates policy and the common technology interface

tables.title: Distinctions and application checks

cells: Direct / indirect taxes
Liability on an income/entity / taxes collected through goods-and-services transactions.
Use the textbook legal distinction without claiming real economic incidence can never shift.
Progressive / proportional / regressive
A rising / constant / falling average burden relative to income.
Rate schedules and distributional outcomes are related but not identical; examine the tax base and spending too.
Ad valorem / specific tax
Based on value / a fixed amount per unit.
Different tax bases imply different responses when prices change; do not confuse tax rate with tax collected.
Cascading / input tax credit
Tax on tax / eligible purchase tax offsets output liability.
Credit depends on conditions; exempt supplies and special schemes cannot automatically be treated as fully creditable.
GST Council / GSTN / collecting authorities
Policy recommendations / common technology interface / tax administration.
Council recommendations, operative law and portal functions are distinct; GST does not subsume every levy.
Tax buoyancy / source's elasticity discussion
Buoyancy = percentage tax-revenue change ÷ percentage GDP change.
Buoyancy alone does not isolate a policy-neutral revenue response; the notes' elasticity/Laffer wording is inconsistent and needs verification.

cards.question: Original illustrative GST calculation: eligible input purchase 1,000 and taxable output sale 1,600, both at an assumed 10%. Find the output liability and net remittance.
cards.answer: Output tax = 160; eligible input credit = 100; net remittance = 60. The invented 10% is not an Indian GST slab. Assume full credit eligibility and no exemption, blocked credit, cross-head adjustment or special-scheme complications; real transactions require current rules.

cards.question: Original illustrative calculation: tax revenue rises from 100 to 115 and nominal GDP from 1,000 to 1,100. Find buoyancy.
cards.answer: Revenue growth = 15%; GDP growth = 10%; buoyancy = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5. Inputs are invented. The result does not prove which part came from rate changes, base changes, enforcement or automatic growth response.

cards.question: Why is 'one nation, one tax' not enough to classify a real transaction?
cards.answer: The notes themselves list levies outside GST and distinguish intra-state and inter-state components. Identify supply and jurisdiction, eligibility/exclusions and applicable law; do not infer that all petroleum, alcohol or every transaction faces one common GST rule.

cards.question: Distinguish evasion, ordinary tax planning and anti-avoidance scrutiny.
cards.answer: Concealing income is evasion; lawful relief use differs from concealment, but a label of 'avoidance' is not blanket protection from anti-abuse rules. The source separately discusses GAAR, residency and treaty/BEPS issues. Use current law for any legal conclusion.

cards.question: How can simpler administration improve a tax system without a higher headline rate?
cards.answer: Clear rules, information matching, source deduction and simpler digital interfaces can reduce compliance friction and support collection. Balance these aims with fairness and administrative cost; do not treat a named historic dispute-settlement window as currently open.

cards.question: Outline: 'A sound tax system must balance adequacy, equity and efficiency.'
cards.answer: Define compulsory, non-quid-pro-quo taxation → design principles and rate patterns → direct/indirect burden → GST credit and federal structure → compliance/anti-abuse and revenue responsiveness → base broadening, certainty and an inclusive reform conclusion.

cards.question: What is the P1 stopping rule for taxation?
cards.answer: Master tax classifications, equity criteria, GST/ITC/inverted-structure logic, institutional roles, buoyancy arithmetic and compliance distinctions. Apply a fresh case and outline. Stop before source-vintage slabs, thresholds and exhaustive reform chronology. Keep mandatory breadth across all syllabus areas; refresh legal numbers only from a dated operative source.

cards.question: What makes these updated notes insufficient as a current tax rulebook?
cards.answer: They combine updated and historical provisions, contradictory angel-tax mentions, simplified GST exclusions and an inconsistent elasticity/Laffer explanation. Some electricity and incidence wording is unreliable. Do not export slabs, registration/composition/audit thresholds, cess status or current statutory applicability from this packet; verify assessment/effective dates and exceptions in official law.
